qt: to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2025/401 (PPWR) applies from 12 August 2026 and was presented as harmonisation for the single market. For the smallest businesses the effect seems to be the opposite. A company sending a parcel to a consumer in another Member State is treated as a producer there. It must register in that country’s producer register, specify the packaging materials used, report quantities and pay fees, separately in each Member State. These costs are largely fixed and do not scale with turnover, so a seller shipping a few parcels a year faces broadly the same administrative overhead as a large retailer. Swedish small businesses have publicly announced that they are closing their online stores to customers in other Member States as of 12 August, because compliance is not viable at their volumes. 1.
Has the Commission assessed the risk that micro-enterprises will stop selling across borders as a result of these obligations?
Has the Commission assessed the cumulative administrative cost borne by a microenterprise registering in several Member States?
Will the Commission examine an exemption from producer registration for SMEs, regardless of the volume of packaging placed on the market?
Regulation (EU) 2025/40 of 19 December 2024 on packaging and packaging waste (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/40/oj). 1
at: (English version) to the Commission Jörgen Warborn (PPE) (12 August 2026) Subject: Administrative burden under Regulation (EU) 2025/40 Regulation (EU) 2025/40 (1) (PPWR) applies from 12 August 2026 and was presented as harmonisation for the single market. For the smallest businesses the effect seems to be the opposite. A company sending a parcel to a consumer in another Member State is treated as a producer there. It must register in that country’s producer register, specify the packaging materials used, report quantities and pay fees, separately in each Member State. These costs are largely fixed and do not scale with turnover, so a seller shipping a few parcels a year faces broadly the same administrative overhead as a large retailer. Swedish small businesses have publicly announced that they are closing their online stores to customers in other Member States as of 12 August, because compliance is not viable at their volumes. 1. Has the Commission assessed the risk that micro-enterprises will stop selling across borders as a result of these obligations? 2. Has the Commission assessed the cumulative administrative cost borne by a micro-enterprise registering in several Member States? 3. Will the Commission examine an exemption from producer registration for SMEs, regardless of the volume of packaging placed on the market? (10 November 2026) To strengthen the Single Market and reduce costs for EU producers, especially Small and Medium-sized Enterprises, the Commission has proposed in its Environmental Omnibus proposal (1) to suspend the obligation for EU producers to appoint an authorised representative (AR) when they conduct direct sale to end users in other Member States. This would immediately alleviate a significant burden for EU producers. In the Staff Working Document (2) for the Environmental Omnibus proposal, which concerns all five extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes, it was estimated that the annual average cost for individual firms to appoint an AR usually varies between several hundred euros and several thousand euros. As regards the registration of producers with EPR schemes, the Commission is working on an Implementing Act under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) (3) to establish harmonised registration and reporting obligations, with a clear focus to keep procedures simple and reduce burden for small and medium-sized companies. Once it is adopted, Member States will have 18 months to establish national registers. Until these registers of producers under the PPWR become operational, producers remain subject to the applicable EPR obligations for registration and reporting established in Member States. The Commission wants to underline the importance of ensuring simple and streamlined procedures during this transitional period. As part of the Circular Economy Act (4), the Commission is preparing a broader reform of EPR schemes, focusing on simplification, harmonisation and digitalisation, which could provide a systemic solution to these matters.
